title: Optimal Fixed Priority Scheduling with Deferred Pre-emption

extraction.paper_name: Optimal Fixed Priority Scheduling with Deferred Pre-emption
extraction.paper_description: This paper introduces an optimal algorithm (FNR-PA) for Fixed Priority Scheduling with Deferred Pre-emption (FPDS). The algorithm determines both the priority ordering of tasks and the lengths of their final non-pre-emptive regions (FNRs) to ensure schedulability. It is optimal in the sense that it finds a schedulable configuration if one exists, and it minimizes blocking from FNRs at every priority level. The paper also provides an analytical method for calculating the minimum FNR length for each task.

formal_description.statement: A taskset comprises n tasks, tau_1, ..., tau_n. Each task tau_i is characterized by its worst-case execution time C_i, minimum inter-arrival time (period) T_i, and relative deadline D_i. The utilization U_i of task tau_i is C_i / T_i. The total utilization U of a taskset is sum(U_i for all tau_i in taskset).

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.T_i: minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i

assumptions: Discrete time model
All task parameters are positive integers
Tasks are sporadic
Single processor
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental characteristics of tasks and tasksets.

informal_sketch.intuition: Tasks are the basic units of work. Each task needs a certain amount of CPU time (C_i), arrives periodically (T_i), and must finish by a certain time (D_i). Utilization measures how much of the CPU a task or the entire system demands.
steps: For each task tau_i:
C_i: How long it takes to run in the worst case.
T_i: Minimum time between consecutive arrivals.
D_i: Time limit from arrival to completion.
U_i = C_i / T_i: Fraction of CPU time task tau_i uses.
Total utilization U = sum(U_i) for all tasks.
key_insights: These parameters are crucial for determining if a task can meet its deadline.
Total utilization U <= 1 is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for schedulability on a single processor.

formal_description.statement: For a given task tau_i, hp_i denotes the set of tasks with priorities strictly higher than tau_i. lp_i denotes the set of tasks with priorities strictly lower than tau_i. hep_i denotes the set of tasks with priorities higher than or equal to tau_i. lep_i denotes the set of tasks with priorities lower than or equal to tau_i.

variables.hp_i: set of tasks with priority higher than i
variables.lp_i: set of tasks with priority lower than i
variables.hep_i: set of tasks with priority higher than or equal to i
variables.lep_i: set of tasks with priority lower than or equal to i

assumptions: Fixed priority scheduling
Task index i represents priority, with 1 being highest and n being lowest
formal_description.conclusion: Defines sets of tasks relative to a given task's priority level.

informal_sketch.intuition: In fixed priority scheduling, tasks are ordered by importance. These sets help identify which tasks can interfere with or be interfered by a specific task.
steps: Assume tasks are indexed 1 to n, where 1 is highest priority and n is lowest.
For task tau_i:
hp_i includes all tasks tau_j where j < i.
lp_i includes all tasks tau_j where j > i.
hep_i includes all tasks tau_j where j <= i.
lep_i includes all tasks tau_j where j >= i.
key_insights: Higher priority tasks can preempt lower priority tasks.
Interference calculations heavily rely on these sets.

formal_description.statement: Under Fixed Priority Scheduling with Deferred Pre-emption (FPDS), each task tau_i has a final non-pre-emptive region of length F_i, where 1 <= F_i <= C_i. This region, once started, executes non-pre-emptively.

variables.F_i: length of the final non-pre-emptive region of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: FPDS scheduling model
F_i is an integer
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the length of the non-pre-emptive tail of a task's execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task can be preempted during most of its execution, but its final F_i time units must run without interruption. This is a configurable parameter for each task.
steps: Identify the last F_i time units of task tau_i's execution.
During this F_i duration, no higher priority task can preempt tau_i.
The value of F_i can range from 1 (fully preemptive, if preemption points are only at the end) to C_i (fully non-preemptive).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Task:
    # ... other attributes ...
    def __init__(self, C, T, D, F=1):
        self.C = C
        self.T = T
        self.D = D
        self.F = F # Final Non-Preemptive Region Length
        # Constraint: 1 <= self.F <= self.C
key_insights: F_i affects both the task's own response time (by reducing preemption) and blocking on higher priority tasks (by increasing non-preemptive execution).
This is a key parameter to optimize for schedulability in FPDS.

results.identifier: Blocking Factor due to Resource Accesses (B_l_i)

formal_description.statement: B_l_i denotes the longest time that a task tau_l in lp_i may execute while holding a resource that is shared with a task of priority i or higher. This represents the longest time for which task tau_l can execute at priority i or higher due to the operation of the Stack Resource Policy (SRP).

variables.B_l_i: longest blocking time imposed by task l on tasks of priority i or higher due to shared resource access
variables.lp_i: set of tasks with priority lower than i

assumptions: Tasks may make mutually exclusive access to shared resources
Stack Resource Policy (SRP) is used
Resource accesses within F_i are properly nested
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum blocking time a lower priority task can impose on a higher priority task due to shared resource contention.

informal_sketch.intuition: Even if a task has higher priority, it can be blocked by a lower priority task if the lower priority task is holding a shared resource that the higher priority task needs. SRP manages this to limit blocking.
steps: Identify all tasks tau_l with lower priority than tau_i (tau_l in lp_i).
For each such tau_l, determine the maximum duration it can hold a resource that tau_i (or any task with priority higher than or equal to tau_i) might need.
This maximum duration is B_l_i.
key_insights: Resource blocking is a critical component of total blocking and affects schedulability.
SRP aims to bound and minimize this blocking.

formal_description.statement: The worst-case response time R_i of a task tau_i is the longest possible time from the release of the task until it completes execution.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i

assumptions: Worst-case scenario of task releases (critical instant)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum time a task takes to complete after its arrival.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the 'actual' time a task takes to finish, considering all delays like preemption, blocking, and interference from other tasks. We want to find the absolute longest this could ever be.
steps: Simulate or analyze the task's execution under the worst possible conditions (e.g., simultaneous release with higher priority tasks, maximum blocking).
Measure the time from its release until its completion.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_worst_case_response_time(task_i, task_set, F_values):
    # This is a complex calculation involving fixed-point iterations
    # (See later formulas for A_i, w_i_g_NP, R_i)
    pass
key_insights: R_i is the primary metric for determining task schedulability.
It must be calculated under a 'critical instant' to find the true worst case.

formal_description.statement: A task tau_i is schedulable if and only if its worst-case response time R_i is less than or equal to its relative deadline D_i (i.e., R_i <= D_i).

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for a single task to meet its timing requirements.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task is 'on time' if it finishes before its deadline. If its worst-case completion time is within its deadline, it's schedulable.
steps: Calculate R_i for task tau_i.
Compare R_i with D_i.
If R_i <= D_i, the task is schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_task_schedulable(task_i, R_i):
    return R_i <= task_i.D
key_insights: This is the fundamental condition for real-time task correctness.
It implies that all jobs of the task will meet their deadlines.

formal_description.statement: A taskset is schedulable if and only if all tasks tau_i in the taskset are schedulable.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for an entire system of tasks to meet its timing requirements.

informal_sketch.intuition: A system is considered schedulable if every single task within it can meet its deadline. One missed deadline means the system is unschedulable.
steps: For each task tau_i in the taskset:
Check if tau_i is schedulable (i.e., R_i <= D_i).
If all tasks are schedulable, then the taskset is schedulable.
key_insights: Schedulability analysis typically aims to determine if a given taskset is schedulable under a specific scheduling policy and parameters.

formal_description.statement: A delta-critical instant for a task tau_i occurs when task tau_i is released simultaneously with all higher priority tasks. Subsequent releases of tau_i and higher priority tasks occur after their minimum permitted time intervals (periods). Further, the minimum possible amount of time delta prior to this simultaneous release, a lower priority task tau_k enters its final non-pre-emptive region or begins accessing a resource shared with a task of priority i or higher. Due to the integer time model, delta is one time unit.
assumptions: Integer time model
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case release pattern and blocking scenario for a task.

informal_sketch.intuition: To find the worst-case response time for a task, we need to consider the absolute worst timing of events. This means the task arrives at the same time as all more important tasks, and it also gets blocked by a lower priority task just before it starts.
steps: Task tau_i and all tasks in hp_i are released at time 0.
Subsequent jobs of these tasks arrive as early as possible (at their periods).
A task tau_k in lp_i starts its FNR or resource access at time -delta (e.g., -1) such that it blocks tau_i at time 0.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def simulate_delta_critical_instant(task_i, task_set):
    # This is a conceptual setup for response time analysis
    # Release all tasks in hep_i at time 0
    # Ensure a lower priority task starts blocking at time -1
    pass
key_insights: The delta-critical instant is fundamental for calculating worst-case response times in FPDS.
It combines the traditional critical instant with the worst-case blocking from lower priority tasks' FNRs or resource accesses.

dependencies: Blocking Factor due to Resource Accesses (B_l_i)

formal_description.statement:
The priority level-i active period A_i is a continuous period of time during which tasks of priority i or higher, that were released at the start of the active period or during it but strictly before its end, are either executing or ready to execute. Its worst-case length is given by the minimum solution to the fixed-point iteration:
`A_i_m_plus_1 = B_i + sum(for all tau_j in hep_i: ceil(A_i_m / T_j) * C_j)`
Iteration starts with `A_i_0 = C_i` and ends when `A_i_m_plus_1 = A_i_m`.

variables.A_i: worst-case length of priority level-i active period
variables.A_i_m: value of A_i at iteration m
variables.B_i: longest time task i can be blocked by lower priority tasks
variables.hep_i: set of tasks with priority higher than or equal to i
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task j

assumptions: Occurs at a delta-critical instant
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum busy period for tasks of priority i and higher.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the longest continuous time interval during which the processor is busy with tasks of priority i or higher. It's like a 'burst' of high-priority work.
steps: Start with an initial estimate for A_i (e.g., A_i_0 = C_i).
In each iteration, calculate the total work that needs to be done by tasks in hep_i within the current A_i estimate, plus the blocking B_i.
The work from higher priority tasks (tau_j in hp_i) is `ceil(A_i_m / T_j) * C_j` (number of jobs * WCET).
The work from task tau_i itself is `ceil(A_i_m / T_i) * C_i`.
The sum of all this work, plus B_i, gives the next estimate A_i_m_plus_1.
Repeat until A_i_m_plus_1 converges to A_i_m.
key_insights: The active period determines how many jobs of a task (and higher priority tasks) can arrive and demand execution within a busy interval.
It's a fundamental building block for response time analysis.

formal_description.statement:
The longest time that task tau_i can be blocked from executing by lower priority tasks is B_i, given by:
`B_i = B_RES_i + B_FNR_i`
where `B_RES_i = max(for all tau_l in lp_i: B_l_i)` is the blocking due to resource locking, and `B_FNR_i = max(for all tau_l in lp_i: F_l)` is the blocking due to final non-pre-emptive regions. The maximum of an empty set is assumed to be zero.

variables.B_i: total blocking factor for task i
variables.B_RES_i: blocking factor due to resource locking for task i
variables.B_FNR_i: blocking factor due to final non-pre-emptive regions for task i
variables.lp_i: set of tasks with priority lower than i
variables.B_l_i: longest blocking time imposed by task l on tasks of priority i or higher due to shared resource access
variables.F_l: length of the final non-pre-emptive region of task l

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total maximum blocking a task can experience from lower priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task can be delayed by lower priority tasks in two main ways: if a lower priority task holds a shared resource (resource blocking), or if a lower priority task is executing its non-preemptive tail (FNR blocking). The total blocking is the sum of these worst-case delays.
steps: Calculate B_RES_i: Find the maximum B_l_i among all tasks tau_l in lp_i. If lp_i is empty, B_RES_i = 0.
Calculate B_FNR_i: Find the maximum F_l among all tasks tau_l in lp_i. If lp_i is empty, B_FNR_i = 0.
B_i = B_RES_i + B_FNR_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_total_blocking(task_i, task_set, F_values, B_l_i_values):
    B_RES_i = 0
    B_FNR_i = 0
    
    lp_i = [task for task in task_set if task.priority > task_i.priority]
    
    if lp_i:
        B_RES_i = max(B_l_i_values[task_l.id] for task_l in lp_i)
        B_FNR_i = max(F_values[task_l.id] for task_l in lp_i)
        
    return B_RES_i + B_FNR_i
key_insights: Blocking is a critical factor in response time analysis, especially in non-preemptive or limited-preemptive scheduling.
The FNR-PA algorithm aims to minimize B_FNR_i.

dependencies: Blocking Factor due to Resource Accesses (B_l_i)

results.identifier: Number of Jobs in Active Period (G_i)

formal_description.statement:
The number of jobs G_i of task tau_i in the priority level-i active period A_i is given by:
`G_i = ceil(A_i / T_i)`

variables.G_i: number of jobs of task i in the active period
variables.A_i: worst-case length of priority level-i active period

formal_description.conclusion: Defines how many jobs of a task contribute to the work within its active period.

informal_sketch.intuition: If an active period lasts for A_i time units, and a task arrives every T_i time units, then `ceil(A_i / T_i)` jobs of that task could potentially arrive and demand execution within that period.
steps: Divide the active period length A_i by the task's period T_i.
Round up to the nearest integer to account for any partial period at the end.
key_insights: G_i is used to iterate through all relevant jobs of a task when calculating its worst-case response time.

results.identifier: Start Time of Final Non-Preemptive Region (w_i_g_NP)

formal_description.statement:
The start time w_i_g_NP of the final non-pre-emptive region of job g (where g = 0 is the first job) of task tau_i, measured with respect to the start of the delta-critical instant, is given by the minimum solution to the fixed-point iteration:
`w_i_g_NP_m_plus_1 = B_i + g * C_i + sum(for all tau_j in hp_i: ceil(w_i_g_NP_m / T_j) * C_j) + F_i`
Iteration starts with `w_i_g_NP_0 = B_i + g * C_i + F_i` and ends when `w_i_g_NP_m_plus_1 = w_i_g_NP_m`. If `w_i_g_NP_m_plus_1 > g * T_i + D_i`, the job is unschedulable.

variables.w_i_g_NP: start time of FNR for job g of task i
variables.w_i_g_NP_m: value of w_i_g_NP at iteration m
variables.B_i: total blocking factor for task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.hp_i: set of tasks with priority higher than i
variables.F_i: length of the final non-pre-emptive region of task i

assumptions: Calculated for jobs within the priority level-i active period
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the earliest possible time a task's final non-pre-emptive region can begin, considering all interference and blocking.

informal_sketch.intuition: This calculation determines when a specific job of a task can finally start its non-preemptive tail. It accounts for all the work that must be done before it, including blocking and higher priority interference.
steps: Initialize w_i_g_NP_0 with the task's own execution (g*C_i), its FNR length (F_i), and total blocking (B_i).
Iteratively add interference from higher priority tasks (hp_i) based on the current estimate of w_i_g_NP_m.
The interference from each higher priority task tau_j is `ceil(w_i_g_NP_m / T_j) * C_j`.
Repeat until the value converges. If it exceeds the job's deadline, the job is unschedulable.
key_insights: This fixed-point iteration is the core of response time analysis for FPDS.
It directly accounts for the non-preemptive nature of the FNR by including F_i in the work term.

formal_description.statement:
The worst-case response time R_i of task tau_i is given by:
`R_i = max(for g from 0 to G_i-1: w_i_g_NP - g * T_i)`
Task tau_i is schedulable provided that `R_i <= D_i`.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.G_i: number of jobs of task i in the active period
variables.w_i_g_NP: start time of FNR for job g of task i

assumptions: w_i_g_NP values are calculated for all jobs g from 0 to G_i-1
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the overall worst-case response time for a task by considering all its jobs within the active period.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's worst-case response time isn't just about its first job; it could be a later job that misses its deadline. We calculate the response time for each job (completion time minus its release time) and take the maximum.
steps: For each job g from 0 to G_i-1:
Calculate w_i_g_NP (the FNR start time).
The job's completion time is w_i_g_NP.
The job's release time is g * T_i.
The job's response time is `w_i_g_NP - g * T_i`.
R_i is the maximum of these individual job response times.
Finally, check if R_i is less than or equal to D_i for schedulability.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_task_response_time(task_i, G_i, w_i_g_NP_values):
    max_R_i = 0
    for g in range(G_i):
        job_completion_time = w_i_g_NP_values[g]
        job_release_time = g * task_i.T
        job_response_time = job_completion_time - job_release_time
        max_R_i = max(max_R_i, job_response_time)
    return max_R_i
key_insights: The worst-case response time can occur for any job within the active period, not just the first.
This formula provides the exact schedulability test for a task under FPDS.

dependencies: Start Time of Final Non-Preemptive Region (w_i_g_NP)
Number of Jobs in Active Period (G_i)

formal_description.statement:
The minimum amount of execution S_i_g_t that task tau_i is certain to be able to perform between the start of its g-th job and some arbitrary time t (prior to that job's deadline) is given by:
`S_i_g_t = max(0, t - B_i - g * C_i - sum(for all tau_j in hp_i: ceil(t / T_j) * C_j))`

variables.S_i_g_t: amount of execution task i, job g, completes by time t
variables.B_i: total blocking factor for task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.hp_i: set of tasks with priority higher than i

assumptions: Measured with respect to the start of the delta-critical instant
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the amount of pre-emptive execution a job can complete by a given time t, considering interference and blocking.

informal_sketch.intuition: This function tells us how much 'useful' work a specific job of a task has managed to do by a certain point in time, after accounting for all delays from blocking and higher priority tasks.
steps: Calculate the total time available for task tau_i up to time t: `t`.
Subtract the blocking B_i.
Subtract the execution of previous jobs of tau_i: `g * C_i`.
Subtract the interference from higher priority tasks (hp_i) up to time t: `sum(ceil(t / T_j) * C_j)`.
The result is the amount of execution tau_i's g-th job has completed. Ensure it's not negative.
key_insights: This is used to determine the minimum FNR length by finding the maximum pre-emptive execution possible while meeting deadlines.

results.identifier: Set of Valid FNR Start Times (P_i_g)

formal_description.statement:
The set of valid start times P_i_g for the final non-pre-emptive region of job g of task tau_i is given by:
`P_i_g = {t | (t >= B_i + g * C_i + sum(for all tau_j in hp_i: ceil(t / T_j) * C_j)) AND (t <= g * T_i + D_i - C_i + S_i_g_t)}`
where `S_i_g_t` is defined as in 'Execution Completed by Time t (S_i_g_t)'.

variables.P_i_g: set of valid FNR start times for job g of task i
variables.B_i: total blocking factor for task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.hp_i: set of tasks with priority higher than i
variables.S_i_g_t: amount of execution task i, job g, completes by time t

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the range of time points where a job's FNR can start such that the job can still complete by its deadline.

informal_sketch.intuition: We're looking for a time 't' where the FNR can start. This 't' must satisfy two conditions: 1) enough pre-emptive work has been done to reach 't' (considering interference and blocking), and 2) if the FNR starts at 't', the entire job (including the remaining pre-emptive part and the FNR) can still finish by its deadline.
steps: Iterate through possible values of 't' (e.g., from 0 up to the job's deadline).
For each 't', calculate S_i_g_t (execution completed by 't').
Check the first inequality: `t` must be greater than or equal to the total work that needs to be done by higher priority tasks and previous jobs, plus blocking, up to time `t`.
Check the second inequality: `t` plus the remaining execution (`C_i - S_i_g_t`) must be less than or equal to the job's absolute deadline (`g * T_i + D_i`).
Any 't' satisfying both is added to P_i_g.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_valid_fnr_start_times(task_i, g, B_i, hp_i):
    P_i_g = []
    deadline_g = g * task_i.T + task_i.D
    
    # Iterate t from 0 up to deadline_g (or a reasonable upper bound)
    # A more efficient approach would check 'schedulable points' as mentioned in paper
    for t in range(0, deadline_g + 1):
        S_i_g_t = calculate_execution_completed(task_i, g, t, B_i, hp_i)
        
        # Condition 1: t >= work_done_by_others_and_self_preemptive_part
        work_before_t = B_i + g * task_i.C
        for task_j in hp_i:
            work_before_t += math.ceil(t / task_j.T) * task_j.C
        
        cond1 = (t >= work_before_t)
        
        # Condition 2: t + (C_i - S_i_g_t) <= deadline_g
        cond2 = (t + (task_i.C - S_i_g_t) <= deadline_g)
        
        if cond1 and cond2:
            P_i_g.append(t)
            
    return P_i_g
key_insights: This set helps identify the flexibility in choosing the FNR start time.
If P_i_g is empty, the job is unschedulable for any FNR length.

results.identifier: Minimum FNR Length for Job g (F_i_g)

formal_description.statement:
The minimum final non-pre-emptive region length F_i_g of the g-th job of task tau_i is given by:
`F_i_g = max(1, C_i - max(for t in P_i_g: S_i_g_t))`
If P_i_g is empty, the job is unschedulable, and F_i_g would be considered infinite or an error.

variables.F_i_g: minimum FNR length for job g of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.P_i_g: set of valid FNR start times for job g of task i
variables.S_i_g_t: amount of execution task i, job g, completes by time t

assumptions: P_i_g is not empty
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the smallest FNR length required for a specific job to meet its deadline.

informal_sketch.intuition: To minimize the FNR length, we want to maximize the amount of pre-emptive execution a job can complete while still meeting its deadline. The FNR then fills the 'gap' between this maximum pre-emptive execution and the total WCET.
steps: Find the maximum value of S_i_g_t for all valid FNR start times 't' in P_i_g.
Subtract this maximum pre-emptive execution from the total WCET C_i. This gives the minimum required FNR length.
Ensure the FNR length is at least 1 (as per definition of F_i).
key_insights: This formula directly links the schedulability conditions to the required FNR length.
It's a crucial step in finding the optimal FNR lengths.

dependencies: Set of Valid FNR Start Times (P_i_g)

results.identifier: Minimum FNR Length for Task i (F_i)

formal_description.statement:
The minimum final non-pre-emptive region length F_i for task tau_i is given by:
`F_i = max(for g from 0 to G_i-1: F_i_g)`
Task tau_i is schedulable provided that `C_i >= F_i`.

variables.F_i: minimum FNR length for task i
variables.G_i: number of jobs of task i in the active period
variables.F_i_g: minimum FNR length for job g of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: F_i_g values are calculated for all jobs g from 0 to G_i-1
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the overall minimum FNR length required for a task to be schedulable, considering all its jobs.

informal_sketch.intuition: Just like response time, the minimum FNR length must satisfy all jobs of a task. If one job needs a longer FNR to be schedulable, then that longer length must be chosen for the task.
steps: Calculate F_i_g for each job g from 0 to G_i-1.
The task's F_i is the maximum of these F_i_g values.
Finally, ensure that the calculated F_i is not greater than C_i (a task's FNR cannot be longer than its total execution time).
key_insights: This provides the 'target' FNR length for a task to ensure its own schedulability.
This value is then used in the FNR-PA algorithm.

Number of Jobs in Active Period (G_i)

formal_description.statement: An algorithm A is said to be optimal for the FNR Problem if there are no taskset / priority assignment combinations that are schedulable under FPDS with some set of values for the lengths of the final non-pre-emptive regions of each task, that are not also schedulable using the set of values for the lengths of final non-pre-emptive regions determined by algorithm A.

variables.A: an algorithm for the FNR Problem
variables.F_values_optimal: set of FNR lengths determined by algorithm A
variables.F_values_any: any other set of FNR lengths

assumptions: Given taskset complies with the task model
Given priority ordering X
formal_description.conclusion: Defines optimality for finding FNR lengths given a fixed priority assignment.

informal_sketch.intuition: If an algorithm is 'optimal' for finding FNR lengths, it means it's as good as it gets. If there's *any* way to make a taskset schedulable by picking FNR lengths (for a given priority order), this optimal algorithm will find those FNR lengths (or an equivalent set) that also make it schedulable.
steps: Assume a taskset and a priority order X are given.
If there exists *any* combination of FNR lengths (F_values_any) that makes the taskset schedulable under FPDS.
Then, an optimal algorithm A must find a combination of FNR lengths (F_values_optimal) that also makes the taskset schedulable.

def is_fnr_algorithm_optimal(algorithm_A, task_set, priority_order_X):

key_insights: Optimality ensures that the algorithm doesn't miss any schedulable solutions.
This definition focuses only on FNR length assignment, assuming priority is fixed.

formal_description.statement: An algorithm B is said to be optimal for the FNR-PA Problem if there are no tasksets compliant with the task model that are schedulable under FPDS with some priority assignment X and some set of values for the lengths of the final non-pre-emptive regions of each task, that are not also schedulable using the priority assignment and set of values for the lengths of the final non-pre-emptive regions determined by algorithm B.

variables.B: an algorithm for the FNR-PA Problem
variables.X_optimal: priority assignment determined by algorithm B
variables.F_values_optimal: set of FNR lengths determined by algorithm B

assumptions: Given taskset complies with the task model
formal_description.conclusion: Defines optimality for finding both priority assignment and FNR lengths.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a stronger form of optimality. If a taskset can be made schedulable by *any* choice of priorities *and* FNR lengths, then an optimal FNR-PA algorithm will find *a* combination of priorities and FNR lengths that makes it schedulable.
steps: If there exists *any* combination of priority assignment (X_any) and FNR lengths (F_values_any) that makes a taskset schedulable under FPDS.
Then, an optimal algorithm B must find *some* priority assignment (X_optimal) and FNR lengths (F_values_optimal) that also makes the taskset schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_fnr_pa_algorithm_optimal(algorithm_B, task_set):
    # Conceptual check for optimality
    # This would involve proving that algorithm_B's output is always schedulable
    # if any schedulable (priority_order, FNR_config) exists for task_set
    pass
key_insights: This is the ultimate goal: finding the best possible configuration for FPDS.
The FNR-PA algorithm presented in the paper aims to achieve this optimality.

results.identifier: Corollary 1: Sustainability of task schedulability with respect to an increase in F_i

formal_description.statement: From the formulas for w_i_g_NP (4) and R_i (5), the worst-case response time R_i of task tau_i is monotonically non-increasing with respect to increases in the length of its final non-pre-emptive region F_i. Stated otherwise, increasing the length of the final non-pre-emptive region of a task cannot result in that task becoming unschedulable if it was previously schedulable.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.F_i: length of the final non-pre-emptive region of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Increasing a task's own FNR length can only improve or maintain its schedulability, not worsen it.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task has a longer non-preemptive tail, it means it's less likely to be interrupted by higher priority tasks during its execution. This reduces its own preemption overheads, which can only help it finish faster or at the same speed, never slower.
steps: Consider a task tau_i with FNR length F_i.
If F_i is increased to F_i_prime (F_i_prime > F_i).
The number of preemptions tau_i experiences can only decrease or stay the same.
This leads to a response time R_i_prime <= R_i.
Therefore, if tau_i was schedulable with F_i (R_i <= D_i), it will remain schedulable with F_i_prime (R_i_prime <= D_i).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_fnr_sustainability(task_i, F_i_old, F_i_new):
    # Assume calculate_task_response_time is available
    R_i_old = calculate_task_response_time(task_i, F_i_old)
    R_i_new = calculate_task_response_time(task_i, F_i_new)
    
    # This corollary states R_i_new <= R_i_old if F_i_new > F_i_old
    assert R_i_new <= R_i_old
    
    if R_i_old <= task_i.D:
        return R_i_new <= task_i.D # Should always be True
key_insights: This property simplifies the search for optimal FNR lengths: if a task is schedulable with a certain F_i, it's also schedulable with any larger F_i.
It implies that when searching for the *minimum* F_i, we can safely increase it if needed without making the task itself unschedulable.

results.identifier: Corollary 2: Sustainability with respect to blocking factor B_k

formal_description.statement: The minimum length for the final non-pre-emptive region F_k of the task at priority level k is monotonically non-decreasing with respect to increases in the blocking factor B_k. Stated otherwise, a larger blocking factor at priority k cannot result in a smaller minimum length for the final non-pre-emptive region of the task at that priority level.

variables.F_k: minimum FNR length for task at priority k
variables.B_k: total blocking factor for task at priority k

formal_description.conclusion: Increasing the blocking a task experiences requires a larger or equal FNR length to maintain its schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task is blocked more, it gets delayed. To compensate for this delay and still meet its deadline, it might need to execute more of its critical section (its FNR) non-preemptively to avoid further interruptions, or it might simply become unschedulable. It definitely won't need a *smaller* FNR.
steps: Consider a task at priority k with blocking B_k and minimum FNR length F_k.
If B_k is increased to B_k_prime (B_k_prime > B_k).
The task's response time will increase, making it harder to meet its deadline.
To counteract this, the task would need to execute more non-preemptively (i.e., F_k would need to increase) or it would become unschedulable.
Therefore, the minimum F_k required will be F_k_prime >= F_k.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_blocking_sustainability(task_k, B_k_old, B_k_new):
    # Assume calculate_min_fnr_for_task is available, which internally uses B_k
    F_k_min_old = calculate_min_fnr_for_task(task_k, B_k_old)
    F_k_min_new = calculate_min_fnr_for_task(task_k, B_k_new)
    
    # This corollary states F_k_min_new >= F_k_min_old if B_k_new > B_k_old
    assert F_k_min_new >= F_k_min_old
key_insights: This property is important for the FNR-PA algorithm, which assigns priorities lowest-first.

When a task is assigned a priority, its blocking from lower priority tasks is fixed. This corollary implies that if a task is moved to a higher priority (reducing its B_k), its required F_k can only decrease or stay the same, which is beneficial.

formal_description.statement: For any taskset where there exists a priority ordering and a set of final non-pre-emptive region lengths that is schedulable under FPDS, the FNR-PA algorithm results in a blocking factor B_FNR_i from final non-pre-emptive regions at every priority level i that is no larger than that obtained with any other schedulable priority and final non-pre-emptive region length assignment.

variables.B_FNR_i: blocking factor due to final non-pre-emptive regions for task i

assumptions: A schedulable solution exists for the taskset under FPDS
formal_description.conclusion: The FNR-PA algorithm finds a schedulable solution that minimizes the FNR-induced blocking at all priority levels.

informal_sketch.intuition: The FNR-PA algorithm is not just optimal in finding *a* schedulable solution, but it's also 'best' in a specific way: it keeps the non-preemptive blocking (from FNRs) as low as possible for all tasks. This is a desirable side-effect because lower blocking generally means better schedulability for higher priority tasks.
steps: The FNR-PA algorithm works by iteratively assigning priorities from lowest to highest.
At each step, it selects the task that can tolerate the shortest FNR length (or is schedulable with the shortest FNR) when placed at the current lowest unassigned priority.
This greedy approach, combined with the properties of FNR length calculation (minimizing F_i for each task), ensures that the overall blocking imposed by lower priority tasks' FNRs is minimized.

The proof (referenced in the paper, but not fully detailed here) involves showing that any deviation from the FNR-PA's choices would lead to an equal or larger blocking factor at some priority level, or an unschedulable system.
